## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dūtajātaka* (Ja 260), titled in English *The Messenger*, is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection. Set at Jetavana, the frame story recounts that the Buddha addressed a monk prone to covetousness, rebuking him by noting that in a past life his excessive greed had caused his head to be cleft with a sword. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*) preserved in the commentary, the Buddha reveals that the greedy man of the past was the covetous monk, whereas the Bodhisatta was the king known as Bhojanasuddhirājā, concluding the first chapter (*Samkappavagga*) [Fausböll 1879].

Modern ethical analysis notes this Jātaka as an instance where the Bodhisatta is depicted as a king who enjoys the luxury and material opulence of royal life rather than renouncing it, an element interpreted didactically to allow the protagonist to connect effectively with his audience [Sahni 2008].
